newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook--Aug aluminium to command attention.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook--Aug aluminium to command attention.

text.p: Base metals started the week on a lively note, particularly aluminium, with August date tightness coinciding with Monday's third Wednesday pricing on the LME, dealers said.
Far East selling and long liquidation sent three month prices spiralling lower early to around $1,660 a tonne, down from Friday's kerb close of $1,702.
Copper should also witness its fair share of activity following Friday's fall to six-month lows as the cash/threes spread moved to a contango for the first time since September 1966.
"There is always plenty of pricing to be done (today)...and you can never tell what will happen, what has been netted out, what is left for the ring," a trader said.
The cash prompt for delivery on the third Wednesday of the month is where volatility is high as open interest gravitates to that date when it is traded as a forward position beyond three months.
"People are increasingly concerned about the August date (in aluminium)," said analyst Martin Squires of LME trader Rudolf Wolff and Co.
This month in aluminium a cluster of tight dates start on Monday, and in the run-up to the pricing last week the August backwardations flared up, as did the benchmark cash/threes premium.
Aug/one day was at $10 backwardation, Aug/one week reached $19, pushing cash/threes to a $30/35 backwardation.
Traders said the tightness was due to bank interests said to be long and lined up against speculative funds and natural trade hedge shorts.

As always, a backwardation sucks in spare metal, and after a long period of drawdowns LME warehouse stocks started rising last week. A total of 9,875 tonnes were put on warrant, although over the year inventories are still down over 300,000 tonnes. On Monday, stocks increased by a further 6,650 tonnes.

Copper traders will be nervous after last Friday's sell-off, when prices fell some $50 in the last 30 minutes of open-outcry trading. The market ended Friday's kerb at $2,213 a tonne, but crumbled below $2,200 in later trading that evening. On early Monday, the market slid to around $2,170.

Sentiment has soured in copper because stocks are rising continually. Partly this is due to the slow summer conditions, but there is also a perception that on a day-to-day basis supply/demand is now in surplus.
Analysts said mine supplies are rising, while refined availability has increased with the Bingham Canyon smelter now working close to name-plate capacity.
Elsewhere, tightness will be a factor in the zinc market, with the cash/threes backwardation racing up to $165/175 last Friday, although the crunch period is still a month away.
Traders say there are still loss-making Chinese short positions in September to be covered.
